proposed_rows.supplier_excerpt:
For a trace-class density $\rho$ with positive eigenvalues $p_i$, define $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_i p_i\log p_i\in[0,\infty]$, with $0\log0=0$. The logarithm is natural and acts on dimensionless density eigenvalues.

For finite-dimensional densities $\rho,\sigma$, define $\operatorname{supp}\rho=(\ker\rho)^\perp$. If $\operatorname{supp}\rho\not\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, set $D(\rho\|\sigma)=+\infty$. Otherwise define
$
D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\sigma),
$
where each logarithm is restricted to the positive support of its operator and zero eigenvalues contribute zero to $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$.

For trace-class normal densities on a separable Hilbert space, write $\rho=\sum_i p_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|$ and $\sigma=\sum_j s_j|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|$ on their positive supports. Define the nonnegative cross-log moment
$
C(\rho,\sigma):=\sum_{i,j}p_i(-\log s_j)|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2\in[0,\infty].
$
This is the spectral first moment of $-\log\sigma$ in the scalar state law of $\rho$; equivalently it is the nonnegative sum over the spectral projections, so it is independent of bases within eigenspaces. When support inclusion holds and $C(\rho,\sigma)$ and $S(\rho)$ are both finite, define $D(\rho\|\sigma)=C(\rho,\sigma)-S(\rho)/k_B$. If $C=+\infty$ and $S(\rho)<\infty$, set $D=+\infty$. No value is assigned by this definition to $+\infty-(+\infty)$; [[thm-qsm-trace-cross-log-inequality]] proves that finite $C$ forces finite $S(\rho)$.

For temperature $T>0$, put $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ and adopt
$
\rho_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta H}}{Z_\beta},\qquad Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H}).
$
In the infinite-dimensional case all scalar energy moments used in a conclusion must also be finite on the actual spectral domain, as required by [[thm-qsm-trace-gibbs-variational]]. With $H$ in joules, $k_B$ in J/K, $T$ in K, and $\beta$ in J$^{-1}$, the exponent is dimensionless and $Z_\beta$ is a dimensionless trace.

This is an adopted preparation rule in the normal-state framework. It is not a theorem that unitary dynamics equilibrates, does not specify a bath or equilibration time, and makes no empirical claim. The finite and trace-Gibbs variational results describe the mathematical optimization associated with this state but do not establish that a physical system is prepared in it.

Put $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta A})$, $\rho_\beta=e^{-\beta A}/Z_\beta$, $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$, and $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_\beta$. Then $Z_\beta\in(0,\infty)$, $\rho_\beta$ is a faithful normal density, and every normal density $\rho$ with finite spectral form energy
$
\mathcal E_A(\rho)=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu_\rho(\lambda),\qquad
\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,d\mu_\rho(\lambda)<\infty,
$
has finite entropy and satisfies
$
\mathcal E_A(\rho)-TS(\rho)\geq F_\beta,
$
with equality exactly at $\rho=\rho_\beta$. The prepared Gibbs state also has
$
S(\rho_\beta)=k_B\bigl(\log Z_\beta+\beta\mathcal E_A(\rho_\beta)\bigr).
$
The trace-class and open-interval hypotheses are essential; a lower bound on $A$ alone does not imply finite $Z_\beta$.
